In the first two parts of this series we [created a plot](https://andrewkates.netlify.app/Posts/2024-08-19-cmj-tracking1/ "Part 1") to visualize jump performance, and then made that plot [interactive](https://andrewkates.netlify.app/Posts/2025-04-01-cmj-tracking2/ "Part 2") in order to better communicate the information to our audience.

```{r}
#| label: setup0
#| echo: false
#| output: false

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(plotly)
library(vroom)

recent_five <- vroom("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AKates717/my-website/refs/heads/master/recent_five.csv") %>%
  mutate(date_mmmddyear = format(Date, "%b %d, %Y"))

ak_plot_theme <- function(..., base_size = 12) {
  theme(
    text = element_text(size = base_size),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "black",
                              face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black",
                             face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust =0.6, vjust = 0.8),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16,
                              color = "black",
                              vjust = 5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "black",
                                 hjust = 0.5),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8,
                                face = "italic",
                                color = "black"),
    panel.grid.major =  element_line(color = "#e0e0e0"),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#ffffff"),
    plot.background = element_blank(),
    panel.border = element_blank())
}

#draw a line between the mean and the max jump height
mean_peak <- function(x) {
  data.frame(y = (mean(x) + 0.0001),
             ymax = max(x),
             ymin = mean(x))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cmj1
#| fig-cap: Interactive Plot Showing Five Most Recent CMJ Assessments
#| echo: false

plot <- recent_five %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), text = date_mmmddyear)) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)


ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>%
    style(hovertemplate = "<b>%{text}</b> <br><i>Mean:</i>  %{y}<extra></extra>", traces = 1) %>% 
    style(text = paste(recent_five$Jump, "\n",
                       recent_five$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>%
    style(text = paste("<b>Five Day Average:</b>",mean(recent_five$flight_height_tov) %>% round(2)), traces = 5) %>%
    style(hoverinfo = "skip", traces = c(2,3)) %>%
    config(displaylogo = FALSE) %>%
    config(modeBarButtonsToRemove = c("hoverCompare", "hoverclosest", "zoomIn2d", "zoomOut2d", "lasso2d"))
```

Now in Part 3, we will add some statistical analysis to our plot, in order to clearly see when jump performance has increased or decreased.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Defining the Approach

> The Question: Is Today's performance meaningfully better or worse than yesterday's performance?

There are several options that we could use to highlight meaningful changes in jump height. In this post I will walk through an example using the Minimal Detectable Change (MDC). MDC can be interpreted as the boundary of measurement error, meaning that any changes in jump height outside of that boundary can be considered a true change [@riemann2018].

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## If the change in jump height between days is greater than the MDC, then that change is not due to measurement error and can be considered a real change in performance.
:::

Here are the steps we will follow in order to visualize changes greater than the MDC on our plot:

1.  **Identify the MDC using historical data for this athlete**

    i.  Identify the Intra-Class Correlation Coefficient (ICC)

    ii. Calculate the Standard Error of Measurement (SEM)

    iii. Calculate the MDC

2.  **Determine when the difference between consecutive daily performances is above or below the MDC.**

3.  **Add a symbol to our interactive plot to indicate potentially real changes in jump height.**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Getting Set Up

If you are starting from scratch and do not have all the data loaded from the [previous](https://andrewkates.netlify.app/Posts/2025-04-01-cmj-tracking2/ "Part 2") post, you will need to open this code, copy it into your R environment, and run the code.

```{r}

library(readxl)

#custom theme
ak_plot_theme <- function(..., base_size = 12) {

    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16,

  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)


ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>%
    style(hovertemplate = "<b>%{text}</b> <br><i>Mean:</i>  %{y}<extra></extra>", traces = 1) %>% 
    style(text = paste(recent_five$Jump, "\n",
                       recent_five$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>%
    style(text = paste("<b>Five Day Average:</b>",mean(recent_five$flight_height_tov) %>% round(2)), traces = 5) %>%

```

Next, we will need to read in some historical data for this fictional athlete, in order to more accurately calculate MDC. Once again, I've created some fictional jump height results which you can find [here](https://github.com/AKates717/my-website/blob/master/Posts/2025-06-01-cmj-tracking3/Athlete1.csv "Athlete1"). Just like with the `recent_five` data we will read the csv into a dataframe, arrange the rows by date, starting with the most recent, and create a new column with a nicely formatted date. As you can see below, the new data set contains 102 jumps.

```{r}
#| output: false

athlete1 <- vroom("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AKates717/my-website/master/Posts/2025-06-01-cmj-tracking3/Athlete1.csv") %>%
  arrange(desc(Date)) %>%
  mutate(date_mmmddyear = format(Date, "%b %d, %Y"))

athlete1
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

athlete1
```

We now have everything we need to proceed with adding MDC analysis to our plot.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 1. Identify the MDC

We will calculate the MDC using the following equations:

$$
\text{SEM} = SD \times\sqrt{1 -ICC}
$$

$$
\text{MDC}_{95} = \text{SEM} \times 1.96 \times \sqrt{2}
$$

For the purposes of this post, we will estimate the ICC for jump height as 0.95. Jump height measured by take-off velocity is typically very reliable, and I have calculated an ICC of 0.98 in the group of athletes I currently work with. I don't think 0.95 is too much of a stretch here, but it should be noted that the higher the ICC is, the lower the SEM and MDC will be. Additionally, note that MDC is being calculated based on the 95% confidence interval and will be represented by MDC~95~ @devet2006 .

The following code will:

1.  Create a new dataframe called `mean_scores` which gives the mean jump height for each day

2.  Use the mean jump heights to calculate the SD, SEM and ultimately the MDC.

```{r}
#| output: false

#Calculate the average jump height per session
mean_scores <- athlete1 %>%
  dplyr::group_by(Date) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(mean_jump_height = mean(flight_height_tov))

#Set ICC
icc <- 0.95

#Calculate SD of session means
sd <- sd(mean_scores$mean_jump_height)

#Calculate SEM
sem <- sd * sqrt(1 - icc)

#Calculate MDC at 95% confidence
mdc <- sem * 1.96 * sqrt(2)
```

This gives us the following values:

$$
\text{SEM} = \text{0.41cm}
$$

$$
\text{MDC}_{95} = \text{1.15cm}
$$

This means that any change in jump height by \> 1.15cm will be considered a real change in performance.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 2. Determine if Change Exceeds MDC

This step involves adding two columns to the `mean_scores` dataframe:

1.  A column displaying the difference between the current day's jump height and the previous one.

2.  A column that returns a symbol ( \* ) whenever the difference score exceeds the MDC.

```{r}

#Add difference scores between consecutive assessment days
mean_scores <- mean_scores %>%
  mutate(diff = c(0, diff(mean_jump_height)))

#Add asterisk if the difference score is greater than the mdc
mean_scores <- mean_scores %>%
  mutate(real = ifelse(abs(diff) > mdc, "*", NA))

```

You should now have a `mean_scores` dataframe that looks like this:

```{r}
#| echo: false
mean_scores
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# 3. Communicate real changes in the plot

Since we are working with the larger data set `athlete1`, which has exactly the same structure as `recent_five` but with more data, let's plot that one first.

The change to the code is actually quite simple, we only need to add one line of code to our original plot. This addition will be a `geom_text` layer which will return the data in `mean_scores$real`. When the difference score is \<1.15cm, the `geom_text` returns `NA` and prints nothing on the plot. When the difference score is \>1.15cm, the `geom_text` will add **`*`**. Run the code below and test it out[^1].

[^1]: Do you see any other differences in this code, compared to our previous plot?

    Since we are plotting a different dataframe, we will also need to change the dataframe in the plotly `style` calls to make sure our tooltips are still providing the correct information.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cmj2
#| fig-cap: Interactive plot including real changes in performance identified using the MDC.
#| echo: true

plot <- athlete1 %>% #<<
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), text = date_mmmddyear)) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  geom_text(data = mean_scores, aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), y = mean_jump_height, label = real), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 8, nudge_x = 0.15) + #<<
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)


ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>%
    style(hovertemplate = "<b>%{text}</b> <br><i>Mean:</i>  %{y}<extra></extra>", traces = 1) %>% 
    style(text = paste(athlete1$Jump, "\n", #<<
                       athlete1$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>% #<<
    style(text = paste("<b>Five Day Average:</b>",mean(athlete1$flight_height_tov) %>% round(2)), traces = 5) %>% #<<
    style(hoverinfo = "skip", traces = c(2,3)) %>%
    config(displaylogo = FALSE) %>%
    config(modeBarButtonsToRemove = c("hoverCompare", "hoverclosest", "zoomIn2d", "zoomOut2d", "lasso2d"))
```

As you can see, the asterisks are there, and as a bonus we have a whole new plot which allows us to visualize trends in jump height over multiple years. However, this plot is a little too messy to clearly see the asterisks, which is the whole point of this post[^2].

[^2]: You could actually just use the Zoom function of the interactive plot to select section of the plot you want to have a closer look at...

Looking at the five most recent jumps on the far right of the plot, I don't see any indications of real changes in jump height at that time. I do see some significant changes in jump height around September 2022, so let's take a look at five assessment dates between Sep 30, 2022 and Feb 16, 2024.

We will just need one additional step of filtering the data in `athlete1` and `mean_scores` to contain only the dates we want to plot. Let's see if we can land this plane.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cmj4
#| fig-cap: Interactive Plot Showing Five Most Recent CMJ Assessments with Stats
#| echo: true

#filter dates #<<
athlete1_filt <- athlete1 %>% #<<
  filter(between(Date, as.Date("2022-09-30"), as.Date("2024-02-16"))) #<<

mean_scores_filt <- mean_scores %>% #<<
  filter(Date %in% athlete1_filt$Date) #<<

plot <- athlete1_filt %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), text = date_mmmddyear)) +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "mean", geom = "point", size = 6, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = Date), fun = "max", geom = "point", size = 4, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov), fun.data=mean_peak, geom="pointrange", size = 2, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  stat_summary(aes(y = flight_height_tov, group = 5), fun = "mean", geom = "line", linewidth = 1, colour = "#D19A2B") +
  geom_jitter(aes(y = flight_height_tov), shape = 1, size = 4, alpha = 0.5, width = 0.2) +
  geom_hline(aes(yintercept = mean(flight_height_tov)), alpha = 0.3, linetype = 2, linewidth = 3) +
  geom_text(data = mean_scores_filt, aes(x = factor(Date, ordered = T), y = mean_jump_height, label = real), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 8, nudge_x = 0.15) + #<<
  ak_plot_theme() +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Jump Height (cm)",
    title = NULL)


ggplotly(plot, tooltip = "text") %>%
    style(hovertemplate = "<b>%{text}</b> <br><i>Mean:</i>  %{y}<extra></extra>", traces = 1) %>% 
    style(text = paste(athlete1_filt$Jump, "\n", #<<
                       athlete1_filt$flight_height_tov), traces = 4) %>% #<<
    style(text = paste("<b>Five Day Average:</b>",mean(athlete1_filt$flight_height_tov) %>% round(2)), traces = 5) %>% #<<
    style(hoverinfo = "skip", traces = c(2,3)) %>%
    config(displaylogo = FALSE) %>%
    config(modeBarButtonsToRemove = c("hoverCompare", "hoverclosest", "zoomIn2d", "zoomOut2d", "lasso2d"))
```

The above plot is a good example of how valuable it can be to use a statistical approach when monitoring jump performance. It seems pretty clear that there was a substantial decrease in performance between Sep 30, 2022 and Nov 02, 2023, however the two subsequent increases in performance are less obvious, and it is helpful to know that these are likely real changes in performance.

Plane Landed.
